lessons.title: PCOS, thyroid antibodies and preconception supplements
lessons.objective: In a woman with PCOS trying to conceive, integrate the initial work-up, the reading of a TSH of 3.2 with positive TPOAb according to ATA, ETA and ASRM, the real place of inositol, and the supported folate and iodine supplements.
lessons.closing: Euthyroid with antibodies: ATA recommends not treating and monitoring every 3–6 months; ETA suggests case-by-case treatment before stimulation. Inositol is experimental as a fertility treatment; letrozole is first line. Folic acid for everyone and iodine if at risk of deficiency, without exceeding 500 µg/day.

lessons.title: Endometrioma, borderline semen and add-ons
lessons.objective: Plan treatment for a couple with an endometrioma and a borderline semen analysis: what to confirm, why not to operate on the endometrioma to improve IVF, when to weigh ICSI, and how to review an add-ons package with ESHRE and NICE.
lessons.closing: Both partners are assessed at once; a borderline semen analysis is repeated at 3 months. The endometrioma is not operated on to improve IVF. Receptivity, immunology, PGT-A, scratching and antioxidants are not supported; hyaluronic acid at transfer is.

lessons.title: Perimenopause, prolactin, “bioidenticals” and commercial tests
lessons.objective: Work up a 44-year-old with irregular cycles, hot flushes and raised prolactin on an antipsychotic, respond to requests for compounded hormones and a stool microbiome test, and decide with her using absolute numbers.
lessons.closing: At 44 it is not POI: NICE allows FSH to be considered. Mild prolactin elevation on an antipsychotic is repeated, causes are reviewed and psychiatry is involved. Approved bioidentical is not compounded. The stool test has no routine use. Every option, including no treatment, in absolute frequencies.

items.title: PCOS and trying to conceive: what to order first
items.core: The 2023 international PCOS guideline diagnoses with two of three criteria after excluding other aetiologies, and when irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism coexist, ultrasound and AMH are not needed. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] For the thyroid, ATA 2026 states that TSH should be measured in every non-pregnant woman with infertility (GPS) and allows TPOAb testing (conditional, low certainty); ETA 2021 recommends TSH and TPOAb in every subfertile woman; and ASRM 2024 asks for TSH and T4 when there are signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism, including irregular cycles, rather than in all patients. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body: In a woman with PCOS and no pre-existing diabetes who is planning pregnancy or seeking fertility treatment, the PCOS guideline proposes considering an oral glucose tolerance test because of the high risk of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] It also asks that, as in any preconception care, weight, blood pressure, smoking, alcohol, diet and nutritional status, folate, exercise, sleep and mental, emotional and sexual health be considered and optimised (consensus, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] ASRM 2024 does not recommend screening asymptomatic infertile women for thyroid autoimmunity, whereas ATA and ETA do contemplate it. [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]] [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]
items.recall: In a woman with PCOS and infertility, what do ATA, ETA and ASRM say about measuring TSH and TPOAb, and which metabolic test does the PCOS guideline propose?
items.pearl: Before ordering TPOAb, decide what you will do with a positive result: that is exactly where the guidelines part ways.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Teede 2023: diagnosis; 1.9.11 (EBR, ❖❖❖, ⊕◯◯◯); 5.1.2 (CR, ❖❖❖❖). ATA 2026, table 4. ETA 2021, R1. ASRM 2024, summary of recommendations.

items.title: TSH 3.2 with positive TPOAb: what each guideline says
items.core: Before pregnancy, ATA 2026 applies the same definitions of normal thyroid function as in the non-pregnant population (GPS) and states that levothyroxine should not be offered to euthyroid women with positive TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility, regardless of TSH or miscarriage history (strong, high certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ETA 2021, by contrast, suggests low-dose levothyroxine (usually 25–50 µg/day) case by case in women with autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0 mIU/L before ovarian stimulation (2, ØØOO). [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] For ASRM 2024, a TSH of 3.2 within the reference range is not subclinical hypothyroidism (it uses the laboratory upper limit or, if none, 4.12 mIU/L), and it does not recommend levothyroxine even for subclinical hypothyroidism in women desiring pregnancy (evidence B, moderate). [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.body: ETA 2021 itself suggests not systematically treating euthyroid women with autoimmunity undergoing IVF/ICSI (R19), and for the R15 case-by-case option it mentions recurrent miscarriage, age > 35 years and ovarian causes of subfertility. [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] ATA 2026 relies on three high-quality trials (TABLET, T4LIFE and a Chinese IVF trial) in which preconception levothyroxine did not improve fertility or pregnancy outcomes. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] ASRM 2024 recommends counselling that a TSH between 2.5 and 4 mIU/L is not associated with more miscarriage (evidence B, moderate). [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]
items.recall: Euthyroid woman with positive TPOAb and TSH 3.2: what does ATA 2026 recommend and what does ETA 2021 suggest?
items.pearl: Put it this way: ATA recommends not treating; ETA suggests case-by-case treatment before stimulation. The recommendation with the highest certainty is ATA’s (strong, high).

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, tables 1 and 7. ETA 2021, R15 and R19 (2, ØØOO). ASRM 2024, definition (p. 767) and summary of recommendations (p. 777). Thyroid and fertility module.

items.title: Positive antibodies: monitor instead of treating
items.core: According to ATA 2026, TPOAb positivity is associated with a 7–9% risk of developing subclinical hypothyroidism before or during pregnancy, and autoimmunity in a euthyroid woman is not an indication for levothyroxine. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] It therefore suggests rechecking TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months while she plans pregnancy (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.body: ATA 2026 states that oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin should not be offered to women with TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility (conditional, low certainty), and in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women it advises against selenium supplements (conditional, moderate certainty). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] If she ever needs levothyroxine, the TSH target in women with infertility is 0.5–2.5 mU/L before and during pregnancy (GPS). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: How often does ATA 2026 suggest rechecking TSH and free T4 in a euthyroid TPOAb-positive woman planning pregnancy, and which treatments does it advise against?
items.pearl: A positive antibody changes how often you check, not what you prescribe.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ATA 2026, tables 4 and 7 (pp. 494 and 497), 7–9% in the text and in the flowchart 1 footnote (p. 501); selenium in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women, table 11 (p. 504; conditional, moderate).

items.title: Inositol: “could be considered” is not “fertility treatment”
items.core: The 2023 international PCOS guideline says that inositol, in any form, could be considered based on preferences and values, noting limited harm, potential improvement in metabolic measures and limited clinical benefit, including in ovulation, hirsutism or weight (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] But in women with PCOS and infertility it states that inositol, alone or combined with other therapies, should be considered experimental therapy, with benefits and risks too uncertain to recommend it as a fertility treatment (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body: The same guideline notes that no specific type, dose or combination of inositol can be recommended, that its side effects and safety are not known, and that these products may have limited regulation, with variable dose, quality and combinations (practice points). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] For ovulation induction in anovulatory women with PCOS and no other infertility factors, the first-line pharmacological treatment is letrozole (strong, high certainty), and lifestyle intervention is recommended for all to improve metabolic health (strong, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: What is the difference between what the PCOS guideline says about inositol in general and about inositol as a fertility treatment?
items.pearl: If she wants to take it, make it an informed choice that does not delay letrozole if she is not ovulating.

items.title: Folate and iodine: what is actually supported
items.core: USPSTF recommends (grade A) that everyone who plans to or could become pregnant take a daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]] The PCOS guideline includes folate in preconception care, with a higher dose if BMI is > 30 kg/m² (without specifying it), and asks for prenatal vitamin supplementation to start together with ovulation induction (consensus and practice point). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body: ATA 2026 recommends that pregnant and lactating women aim for a daily iodine intake of 250 µg, from diet plus supplements as required (strong, moderate), and suggests a 150 µg/day supplement, ideally from at least 3 months before pregnancy until lactation is complete, in women at risk of deficiency because of geographic region, dietary restrictions or malabsorption (conditional, moderate). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] It also asks to avoid sustained excessive iodine intake and supplements above 500 µg/day in pregnancy, because of concerns for fetal and maternal thyroid dysfunction (strong, moderate). [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]
items.recall: What folic acid dose does USPSTF recommend, and to whom does ATA 2026 suggest a 150 µg/day iodine supplement?
items.pearl: When reviewing her “PCOS” multivitamin, add up the iodine from every supplement she takes.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: USPSTF 2023 (grade A). Teede 2023: 5.1.2 (CR, ❖❖❖❖) and practice point on prenatal vitamins. ATA 2026, table 3.

items.stem: Olga (fictional case), 31, with PCOS, is trying to conceive without assisted reproduction. TSH 3.2 mU/L within her laboratory range, normal free T4 and positive TPOAb. What does ATA 2026 state?

options.text: Levothyroxine to bring TSH below 2.5 mU/L
options.why: The 0.5–2.5 mU/L target is for women already on levothyroxine; in a euthyroid antibody-positive woman ATA says not to treat, whatever the TSH.

options.text: Do not offer levothyroxine, regardless of TSH within the normal range
options.why: Correct: a strong, high-certainty recommendation for euthyroid women with TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility.

options.text: Selenium to lower the antibodies
options.why: ATA advises against selenium in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate); it does not propose it as treatment.

options.text: Low-dose oral prednisolone
options.why: ATA states that prednisolone or immunoglobulin should not be offered to antibody-positive women with infertility.

items.explanation: Before pregnancy ATA uses the non-pregnant definitions, so a TSH within range is euthyroidism. With positive antibodies, what changes is follow-up (TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months), not treatment.

items.stem: Which of these statements about thyroid and fertility guidelines is correct?

options.text: ASRM 2024 recommends TPOAb testing in every woman with infertility
options.why: The opposite: ASRM does not recommend screening asymptomatic infertile women for autoimmunity; ETA is the one recommending it in every subfertile woman.

options.text: ATA 2026 suggests levothyroxine with positive TPOAb if TSH exceeds 2.5 mU/L
options.why: ATA says levothyroxine should not be offered to euthyroid antibody-positive women with infertility, regardless of TSH.

options.text: ETA 2021 suggests case-by-case low-dose levothyroxine with autoimmunity and TSH 2.5–4.0 before stimulation, and ASRM 2024 does not recommend treating subclinical hypothyroidism in women desiring pregnancy
options.why: Correct: this is the real disagreement; ETA (R15, 2, ØØOO) predates T4LIFE.

options.text: All three guidelines agree on not measuring TSH unless there are symptoms
options.why: ATA (GPS) and ETA measure TSH in all women with infertility; only ASRM limits it to signs or symptoms, which include irregular cycles.

items.explanation: ATA recommends not treating euthyroid antibody-positive women; ETA suggests case-by-case treatment before stimulation; ASRM recommends neither treating subclinical hypothyroidism nor screening asymptomatic women for autoimmunity.

items.stem: Olga asks whether an inositol product will help her get pregnant. According to the 2023 international PCOS guideline, what is correct?

options.text: It is first-line treatment before letrozole
options.why: First-line pharmacological ovulation induction is letrozole (strong, high certainty).

options.text: As a fertility treatment it should be considered experimental, with benefits and risks too uncertain
options.why: Correct: recommendation 5.8.1 (conditional, very low certainty).

options.text: A specific ratio of myo- and D-chiro-inositol is recommended
options.why: The guideline says no specific type, dose or combination can be recommended because of a lack of quality evidence.

options.text: It is contraindicated because of proven harm
options.why: The guideline speaks of limited harm and unknown safety, not proven harm.

items.explanation: The guideline separates two uses: in general, inositol could be considered according to preferences (limited clinical benefit); as a fertility treatment it is experimental. If she takes it, she should tell her clinicians and know that quality and dose of these products can vary.

items.stem: Olga follows a strict vegan diet and hardly uses iodised salt. Which iodine advice fits ATA 2026?

options.text: 150 µg/day supplement, ideally from at least 3 months before pregnancy
options.why: Correct: ATA suggests it for women at risk of deficiency because of dietary restrictions (conditional, moderate).

options.text: 1000 µg/day “to support the thyroid” because of her antibodies
options.why: ATA asks to avoid supplements above 500 µg/day in pregnancy (strong, moderate).

options.text: No iodine until she has a positive pregnancy test
options.why: ATA proposes starting ideally at least 3 months before pregnancy.

items.explanation: Dietary restriction is one of the deficiency risks named by ATA. The goal in pregnancy and lactation is an intake of 250 µg/day from diet plus supplements, without exceeding 500 µg/day from supplements. The ATA text adds that a vegan diet may require somewhat larger amounts, always within that ceiling.

items.title: Case: Olga, PCOS, thyroid antibodies and inositol

steps.text: Olga (fictional case), 31, has been trying to conceive for 14 months; her cycles last 35 to 60 days and she has hirsutism. With irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism, the PCOS diagnosis needs neither ultrasound nor AMH, but other aetiologies must be excluded; the PCOS guideline also proposes considering an oral glucose tolerance test when planning pregnancy. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] You order TSH, as ATA indicates for every woman with infertility and ASRM for irregular cycles, and TPOAb, which ATA allows and ETA recommends. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]]

Results: TSH 3.2 mU/L within the laboratory range, normal free T4 and positive TPOAb. With the non-pregnant definitions that ATA applies before pregnancy, Olga is euthyroid, and ATA states that levothyroxine should not be offered in this situation, regardless of TSH. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

A friend told her that with antibodies “you have to take thyroid pills”. You explain the disagreement: ATA recommends not treating; ETA suggests case-by-case low-dose levothyroxine with TSH 2.5–4.0 before ovarian stimulation; for ASRM, a TSH of 3.2 within range is not subclinical hypothyroidism, it recommends counselling that a TSH of 2.5–4 is not associated with more miscarriage, and it does not recommend levothyroxine even for subclinical hypothyroidism. [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]] [[ref:eta-2021-thyroid-art]] [[ref:asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism]]

Olga brings an inositol product “for fertility”. The PCOS guideline considers it experimental as a fertility treatment, with no recommendable type or dose and unknown safety. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

She is a strict vegan. You advise folic acid 0.4–0.8 mg/day, as USPSTF recommends, and consider iodine: ATA suggests 150 µg/day in women with dietary restrictions and asks not to exceed 500 µg/day from supplements in pregnancy. [[ref:uspstf-2023-folic-acid]] [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

Plan: lifestyle according to the PCOS guideline, letrozole as first line if anovulation is confirmed with no other factors, a semen analysis for her partner as part of assessing both at once, and TSH with free T4 every 3–6 months while she tries to conceive. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy]]

items.title: Endometrioma and IVF: no surgery to “improve IVF”
items.core: ESHRE 2022 does not recommend routine surgery for an endometrioma before assisted reproduction to improve live birth, because the evidence shows no benefit and surgery probably reduces ovarian reserve (strong, ⊕⊕); it may be considered to treat pain or improve follicle access (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] Nor does it recommend ovarian suppression to improve fertility (strong, ⊕⊕) or extended GnRH agonist administration before assisted reproduction (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body: If the couple prefers to try for a spontaneous pregnancy, ESHRE says operative laparoscopy may be considered for endometrioma-associated infertility, although no comparative studies exist (weak, ⊕), with specific caution to minimise ovarian damage (strong, ⊕); NICE offers cystectomy or drainage and ablation, taking into account the possible impact on ovarian reserve (1.10.2). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] NICE advises against hormonal treatment, alone or with surgery, for people trying to conceive (1.10.4). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Why does ESHRE not recommend routine endometrioma surgery before IVF, and when may it be considered?
items.pearl: The question for an endometrioma before IVF is “does it hurt or block retrieval?”, not “will it improve IVF?”.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, recommendations 28, 39, 44, 53, 56 and 57; NICE NG73 1.10.2 and 1.10.4. Endometriosis and fertility module.

items.title: A “borderline” semen analysis: repeat and assess both partners
items.core: The WHO 2021 reference limits are the 5th centile of men whose partners conceived within 12 months: for example, concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml and progressive motility 30%. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]] AUA/ASRM points out that semen analysis cannot precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men except in azoospermia and some extreme pictures, recommends assessing both partners concurrently (expert opinion) and including one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (strong; evidence B). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.body: If the first semen analysis is abnormal, NICE offers a repeat, ideally at 3 months to allow the cycle of sperm formation to be completed, except in azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, when it is repeated as soon as possible (1.17.3–1.17.4). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] With 2 or more abnormal analyses, NICE offers examination of the scrotum and testes and suggests considering testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] NICE suggests considering ICSI if semen parameters are abnormal, taking severity into account, and not using it without male factor if semen is normal (1.50.2–1.50.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What do the WHO 2021 limits mean, and when does NICE propose repeating an abnormal semen analysis?
items.pearl: A value just below the 5th centile is a finding to confirm, not a diagnosis.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WHO 2021, reference limits table. AUA/ASRM 2020. NICE NG257 1.17.3–1.17.5 and 1.50.2–1.50.3. Male factor module.

items.title: Endometriosis plus male factor: when assisted reproduction
items.core: ESHRE 2022 states that assisted reproduction can be used for endometriosis-associated infertility, especially if tubal function is compromised, there is male factor, the EFI is low or other treatments have failed (weak, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] It does not recommend a specific protocol: GnRH antagonist or agonist according to preferences, as no difference in pregnancy or live birth has been shown (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body: The ESHRE add-ons document does not recommend ICSI without male factor (“not recommended”), and NICE reserves it for abnormal semen according to severity or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] For male factor, AUA/ASRM considers supplements such as antioxidants and vitamins of questionable clinical utility, with data that do not allow recommending specific agents (moderate; grade B). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: In which situations does ESHRE 2022 point to assisted reproduction in endometriosis, and when does NICE suggest considering ICSI?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, recommendation 49 and protocol; ESHRE add-ons 2023 (ICSI without male factor); NICE NG257 1.50.2; AUA/ASRM 2020.

items.title: The “extras” package: what ESHRE and NICE say
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend the currently available endometrial receptivity tests or peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing (“not recommended”), and considers PGT-A and endometrial scratching “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”; NICE advises not to offer receptivity testing, PGT-A to improve live birth or scratching as pre-treatment (1.41.1, 1.48.1 and 1.40.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] For the man, ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction, and NICE advises against sperm DNA fragmentation testing (1.17.6). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body: Not everything is rejected: ESHRE recommends adding hyaluronic acid to the transfer medium (“recommended”), combined with a single embryo transfer policy. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] It also asks that every test or intervention be evaluated for efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness, that this evaluation become a standard part of counselling, and that only evidence-based add-ons be offered in clinical practice; of its 42 recommendations, none rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: In a package with receptivity testing, NK cells, PGT-A, scratching, antioxidants and hyaluronic acid, which element does ESHRE recommend?
items.pearl: Go through the package line by line with ESHRE’s four phrases: the “yes” to hyaluronic acid and the “no” to immune tests then become equally clear.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023 (receptivity, immunology, PGT-A, scratching, antioxidants, hyaluronic acid, counselling). NICE NG257 1.17.6, 1.40.1, 1.41.1 and 1.48.1. Add-ons module.

items.stem: Silvia (fictional case), 36, has a 4 cm left endometrioma without pain and is about to start IVF. She is offered a cystectomy first “to improve results”. According to ESHRE 2022, what is correct?

options.text: Routine surgery improves live birth and is recommended
options.why: ESHRE says the opposite: it shows no benefit and probably reduces ovarian reserve.

options.text: Routine surgery to improve live birth is not recommended; it may be considered for pain or follicle access
options.why: Correct: a strong recommendation (⊕⊕) plus a GPP for the other indications.

options.text: Better 3–6 months of GnRH agonist before IVF
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend extended GnRH agonist before assisted reproduction because the benefit is uncertain (strong, ⊕).

options.text: Operate only if AMH is high
options.why: ESHRE does not frame the indication this way: surgery before IVF is considered for pain or follicle access.

items.explanation: Endometrioma surgery before assisted reproduction does not improve live birth and probably reduces ovarian reserve. With no pain and accessible follicles, there is no indication to operate to “improve IVF”.

items.stem: Óscar, Silvia’s partner, has a concentration of 14 × 10⁶/ml on his first semen analysis, with all other parameters above the WHO 2021 limits. What is correct?

options.text: It confirms male infertility and mandates ICSI
options.why: Semen analysis cannot precisely separate fertile from infertile men except in extreme cases, and NICE asks for a confirmatory analysis.

options.text: It is below the 5th reference centile; repeat it, ideally at 3 months
options.why: Correct: the concentration limit is 16 × 10⁶/ml and NICE repeats ideally at 3 months.

options.text: It is normal by the WHO 6th edition and can be ignored
options.why: The 6th-edition limit is 16 × 10⁶/ml, so 14 lies below it.

options.text: Routinely order DNA fragmentation and scrotal ultrasound
options.why: NICE advises against fragmentation testing, and AUA/ASRM does not recommend routine scrotal ultrasound in the initial evaluation.

items.explanation: A value below the 5th centile is confirmed before labelling it. If 2 or more analyses are abnormal, NICE adds examination and consideration of testosterone and gonadotrophins.

items.stem: The clinic offers Silvia and Óscar a package with endometrial receptivity testing, uterine NK-cell testing, PGT-A and hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium. Which element does ESHRE 2023 recommend?

options.text: Endometrial receptivity testing
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend it and NICE advises not to offer it (1.41.1).

options.text: Uterine NK-cell testing
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend immune tests or uterine NK-cell testing.

options.text: PGT-A
options.why: ESHRE considers it “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” and NICE advises not to offer it to improve live birth.

options.text: Hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium
options.why: Correct: it is “recommended”, combined with single embryo transfer.

items.explanation: Appraising a package means going item by item: the same guideline that rejects receptivity and immune testing recommends hyaluronic acid.

items.title: Case: Silvia and Óscar, endometrioma, borderline semen and an extras package

steps.text: Silvia (fictional case), 36, and Óscar, 38, have been trying to conceive for 2 years. Silvia has a painless 4 cm left endometrioma; Óscar’s first semen analysis shows 14 × 10⁶/ml with all other parameters normal. You assess both at once, as AUA/ASRM recommends, and compare with the WHO 2021 limits. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

The concentration is below the 5th centile, but semen analysis cannot precisely separate fertile from infertile men; NICE repeats the analysis ideally at 3 months. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

The repeat confirms a mild reduction. With endometriosis and male factor, ESHRE considers assisted reproduction (weak, ⊕⊕), and NICE suggests weighing ICSI according to the severity of the semen abnormality. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

They are offered surgery on the endometrioma first “to improve IVF”. ESHRE does not recommend it routinely: it shows no live-birth benefit and probably reduces ovarian reserve; with no pain or follicle access problems, there is no other indication. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

The clinic adds a package: receptivity testing, NK cells, PGT-A, scratching, antioxidants for Óscar and hyaluronic acid at transfer. You go through it item by item with the ESHRE add-ons document and NICE NG257. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

You discuss it with both of them following NICE NG197: aim, benefits, risks and consequences of each option, including doing nothing, and separating with ESHRE what has shown benefit from what has not. They choose IVF without prior surgery or extras, except the hyaluronic acid the laboratory offers. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

items.title: 44, irregular cycles and hot flushes: neither POI nor “menopause without tests”
items.core: The 2024 ESHRE guideline defines premature ovarian insufficiency as loss of ovarian activity before age 40; it calls cessation of ovarian function between 40 and 44 early menopause, which is outside its scope. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]] NICE identifies perimenopause without tests from age 45, and between 40 and 45, with symptoms including a change in the menstrual cycle, it proposes considering serum FSH to confirm menopause (1.3.6). [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body: NICE advises against using FSH to identify menopause in people using combined hormonal contraception or high-dose progestogen (1.3.5), and from age 45 against using AMH, inhibins, estradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume (1.3.4). [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] Irregular cycles have another possible explanation here: hyperprolactinaemia causes oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, with or without galactorrhoea. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: Between 40 and 45 with symptoms and cycle change, which test does NICE propose considering, and in whom should it not be used?
items.pearl: At 44, think along two lines at once: the menopause transition and any other cause of the cycle change.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2024 POI, definition and scope. NICE NG23 1.3.4–1.3.6 [2015]. Pituitary Society 2023 (hyperprolactinaemia and oligo/amenorrhoea, p. 723).

items.title: High prolactin on an antipsychotic: the likeliest causes first
items.core: The 2023 Pituitary Society consensus recommends rigorously reviewing medication to exclude drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia, recognising primary hypothyroidism and renal and liver failure as causes of mild elevations, and not overlooking pregnancy (all strong); in addition, values below five times the upper limit of normal should be repeated (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] Hyperprolactinaemia occurs in 30–75% of people receiving antipsychotics within the first 3 months, with elevations of up to ten times the upper limit described; above ten times, a prolactinoma should be suspected (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.body: The consensus indicates MRI in people on antipsychotics if prolactin exceeds ten times the upper limit, there are mass-effect symptoms such as headache or visual disturbance, or there are pituitary deficiencies other than the gonadal axis; dose reduction or switching to a second-generation antipsychotic that does not raise prolactin, such as aripiprazole, distinguishes prolactinoma from the drug cause in most patients (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]] By extension, that switch is coordinated with psychiatry: the consensus asks for collaboration between endocrinology, neurosurgery and psychiatry to manage a prolactinoma in people with a psychiatric disorder (strong). [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]
items.recall: In a woman on an antipsychotic with raised prolactin, which causes must be reviewed, which level raises suspicion of prolactinoma, and when is MRI ordered?
items.pearl: Never stop the antipsychotic yourself to “clarify” a prolactin result: the conversation starts with her psychiatrist.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Pituitary Society 2023: initial assessment (repeat if < 5 × ULN; causes) and the psychiatric disorder section. Prolactin module.

items.title: “Bioidentical”: approved hormones versus compounded preparations
items.core: NAMS 2022 warns that “bioidentical” can mislead: there are approved, regulated bioidentical hormones (estradiol, estrone and micronized progesterone) and compounded preparations that may combine several hormones in untested combinations, formulations or routes, such as subdermal implants, pellets or troches. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] Compounded preparations raise safety concerns: minimal regulation and monitoring, overdosing and underdosing, impurities and lack of sterility, lack of efficacy and safety data, and no label outlining risks (Level I). [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body: NAMS considers salivary and urine hormone testing to set doses unreliable and does not recommend it (Level II/III), and states that patient preference alone does not justify a compounded preparation, particularly when regulated bioidentical hormones are available (Level III); they are only considered for allergy to an ingredient of an approved product or a dose that is not available (Level III). [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] For vasomotor symptoms, NICE recommends offering HRT, combined HRT for people with a uterus. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: Which approved bioidentical hormones does NAMS list, and which safety concerns does it attribute to compounded preparations?
items.pearl: If what she wants is “natural”, you can offer approved estradiol and micronized progesterone: bioidentical and regulated.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NAMS 2022, compounded bioidentical hormones section and key points (Levels I, II/III and III). NICE NG23 (HRT for vasomotor symptoms; combined with a uterus).

items.title: Stool microbiome test: what the international consensus says
items.core: The 2025 international consensus on microbiome testing concludes that there is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine use in clinical practice (90% agreement) and discourages patients from requesting tests directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] It also discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice in the report (98%) and states that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.body: The same consensus states that there is generally not enough information to report strict “healthy” reference ranges for species abundance (90%), discourages the Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio (86%) and considers the evidence insufficient to include dysbiosis indices (90%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]] In addition, patients should not suspend their therapy or change their diet before testing unless the referring physician recommends it (100%). [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]
items.recall: What does the 2025 consensus say about routine microbiome testing, direct patient requests and therapeutic advice in the report?
items.pearl: A report that comes with its own supplement plan already goes against what the consensus asks.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Porcari et al. 2025, statements 3, 6, 8, 26, 27, 28, 30 and 32 (Delphi, 69 experts). Microbiota and evidence modules.

items.title: Deciding with her: every option, including doing nothing, and with numbers
items.core: NICE NG197 defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which a person and their professional reach a decision together, and asks to explain the aim of each option, openly discuss the risks, benefits and consequences of each, including no treatment or no change, clarify what the person hopes to gain, and discuss misconceptions. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] It recommends using numerical data when available, as absolute risk, with natural frequencies and the same denominator when comparing. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]]
items.body: NAMS considers absolute risk more useful than relative risk for conveying benefits and risks in clinic, and places the most favourable balance of hormone therapy in women who start it before 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, without contraindications. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] For vasomotor symptoms, NICE recommends offering HRT and considering menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy as an option, including when the person prefers not to take hormones. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: According to NICE NG197, which options must always be discussed, and how should numbers be presented?
items.pearl: “What you are asking for has no safety data; what I am offering does. What worries you most about hormones?”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG197, definition, 1.2.10 and 1.4.6–1.4.9. NAMS 2022 (absolute risk and timing window). NICE NG23 (HRT and CBT for vasomotor symptoms).

items.stem: Mercedes (fictional case), 44, not using hormonal contraception, has had irregular cycles for 8 months and hot flushes. According to NICE NG23, what is correct?

options.text: Diagnose premature ovarian insufficiency with an FSH > 25 IU/L
options.why: POI is before 40; if ovarian function ceases between 40 and 44, it is called early menopause.

options.text: Serum FSH may be considered to confirm menopause
options.why: Correct: NICE proposes it between 40 and 45 with symptoms, including a change in the cycle (1.3.6).

options.text: Order AMH to diagnose perimenopause
options.why: NICE does not include AMH for this: it advises against it from 45, and between 40 and 45 it only contemplates FSH.

options.text: Order no tests at all, as from age 45
options.why: Identification without tests applies to people aged 45 or over.

items.explanation: Between 40 and 45, NICE proposes considering FSH to confirm menopause if there are symptoms and cycle changes, except with combined contraception or high-dose progestogen. In Mercedes, the raised prolactin also forces you to consider another cause of the cycle change.

items.stem: Mercedes has been on an antipsychotic for years. Her prolactin is twice the upper limit, with no headache or visual disturbance. What next step best fits the 2023 Pituitary Society consensus?

options.text: Urgent pituitary MRI
options.why: In people on antipsychotics, the consensus indicates MRI with prolactin > 10 times the limit, mass-effect symptoms or other pituitary deficiencies; at twice the limit and without mass-effect symptoms, there is no reason for an urgent MRI.

options.text: Start cabergoline now
options.why: The value must first be confirmed and drug and systemic causes excluded.

options.text: Repeat prolactin, rule out pregnancy, hypothyroidism and renal or liver failure, and review with psychiatry
options.why: Correct: values < 5 times the limit are repeated, and reviewing causes is a strong recommendation.

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic yourself for 4 days and repeat
options.why: Any antipsychotic change is coordinated with her psychiatrist; the consensus asks for that collaboration in prolactinoma with a psychiatric disorder, and the same logic applies here.

items.explanation: Elevations of up to ten times the limit are described with antipsychotics. At twice the limit, the first step is to confirm and review causes; if the origin must be clarified, reducing or switching the antipsychotic is done with her psychiatrist.

items.stem: Mercedes wants compounded “bioidentical” hormone pellets, with the dose set by a saliva test. What is consistent with NAMS 2022?

options.text: They are safer because they are identical to her own
options.why: NAMS describes safety concerns with compounded preparations and a lack of efficacy and safety data (Level I).

options.text: The saliva test allows precise dosing
options.why: NAMS considers saliva and urine testing for dosing unreliable and does not recommend it.

options.text: Her preference is enough to prescribe them
options.why: Preference alone does not justify a compounded preparation, particularly when regulated bioidentical options exist (Level III).

options.text: Offer approved estradiol and micronized progesterone, and reserve compounded products for allergies or unavailable doses
options.why: Correct: they are regulated bioidentical hormones, and those are the situations in which NAMS considers a compounded product.

items.explanation: “Bioidentical” is not a synonym for compounded. Approved bioidentical hormones are regulated; compounded products have dose and purity problems and lack data, and saliva-based dosing is unreliable.

items.stem: Mercedes brings a stool microbiome test that promises her a personalised supplement plan “to balance her hormones”. What is consistent with the 2025 international consensus?

options.text: It is useful if the laboratory provides healthy reference ranges
options.why: The consensus says there is generally not enough information to report strict reference ranges (90%).

options.text: The Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio guides the probiotic
options.why: The consensus discourages reporting that ratio (86%).

options.text: She should stop her medication before the test for a cleaner result
options.why: She should not suspend therapy unless the referring physician recommends it (100%).

options.text: There is insufficient evidence for routine use, and therapeutic advice in the report is discouraged
options.why: Correct: statements 32 (90%) and 30 (98%).

items.explanation: The consensus sees insufficient evidence for routine use, discourages direct requests without a clinical recommendation and the provider including treatment in the report: any change is decided by the referring professional.

items.title: Case: Mercedes, 44, hot flushes, high prolactin, “bioidenticals” and a stool test

steps.text: Mercedes (fictional case), 44, not using hormonal contraception, has had irregular cycles for 8 months and hot flushes. At her age this is not POI, and NICE proposes considering FSH to confirm menopause between 40 and 45 with symptoms and cycle change. [[ref:eshre-2024-poi]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

She has been on an antipsychotic for years, and her GP found a prolactin of twice the upper limit, with no headache or visual disturbance. Oligo/amenorrhoea can be a symptom of hyperprolactinaemia, and the Pituitary Society consensus asks to repeat values below five times the limit and to review drugs, pregnancy, thyroid, kidney and liver. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

The pregnancy test is negative, TSH and renal and liver function are normal, and the repeat prolactin remains around twice the limit. Elevations of up to ten times the limit are described with antipsychotics, Mercedes has neither prolactin > 10 times the limit nor mass-effect symptoms; if there is also no evidence of deficiencies in other pituitary axes (the consensus’s third criterion for MRI), she does not need it for now, and you discuss it with her psychiatrist. [[ref:petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus]]

For the hot flushes she asks for compounded “bioidentical” pellets dosed by saliva. NAMS describes their safety concerns, does not recommend saliva-based dosing and states that preference alone does not justify them when regulated bioidentical options exist. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

She also brings a stool microbiome test with a supplement plan. The 2025 international consensus sees insufficient evidence for routine use and discourages therapeutic advice in the report. [[ref:porcari-2025-microbiome-testing]]

You decide with her following NICE NG197: HRT with approved estradiol and micronized progesterone (combined, because she has a uterus), cognitive behavioural therapy, or no treatment for now, with risks given as absolute frequencies; as she still has cycles, you also give her information about contraception. She chooses to try approved HRT, with a review at 3 months, and to drop the stool test. [[ref:nice-2021-ng197]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman (fictional case) with PCOS and no pre-existing diabetes is about to try to conceive. Besides preconception care, which metabolic test does the 2023 international PCOS guideline propose considering?

options.text: An isolated HbA1c, which the guideline prefers to any other test because it needs no fasting or glucose load
options.why: The guideline proposes considering an oral glucose tolerance test because of the high risk of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy.

options.text: Fasting insulin with HOMA index, which according to the guideline is the test of choice to decide on adding metformin before pregnancy
options.why: The guideline does not propose that test in this setting.

options.text: An oral glucose tolerance test, because of the high risk of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy (conditional, very low certainty)
options.why: Correct: this is the guideline’s proposal for women planning pregnancy or fertility treatment.

options.text: None, because the guideline considers that PCOS metabolic risk should be assessed only after delivery and not before conception
options.why: The guideline does propose considering the glucose tolerance test before pregnancy.

items.explanation: In women with PCOS and no pre-existing diabetes who are planning pregnancy or seeking fertility treatment, the 2023 PCOS guideline proposes considering an oral glucose tolerance test because of the high risk of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy (conditional, very low certainty), and asks for weight, blood pressure, smoking, alcohol, diet, folate, exercise, sleep and mental, emotional and sexual health to be optimised (consensus, strong).

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman (fictional case) has 40–90-day cycles and clinical hirsutism; other aetiologies have been excluded. Under the 2023 PCOS guideline, are ultrasound or AMH needed to diagnose PCOS?

options.text: No: with irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism she already meets two of three criteria, and ultrasound and AMH are not needed
options.why: Correct: this is what the guideline states.

options.text: Yes: AMH is mandatory in every woman, because the guideline considers it the main criterion, replacing irregular cycles
options.why: AMH is an alternative to ultrasound for the morphology criterion, not a mandatory criterion.

options.text: Yes: ultrasound is essential in every case, because without polycystic ovarian morphology PCOS cannot be diagnosed
options.why: Two of three criteria are enough; morphology is not mandatory.

options.text: No, but only because the guideline allows PCOS to be diagnosed with a single criterion when that criterion is clinical hyperandrogenism
options.why: Two of three criteria are needed, not one.

items.explanation: The 2023 international PCOS guideline diagnoses with two of three criteria after excluding other aetiologies; when irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism coexist, ultrasound and AMH are not needed.

items.stem: Which pairing of guideline and position on thyroid testing in women with infertility is correct?

options.text: ASRM 2024: TSH and TPOAb in every woman with infertility, because it considers thyroid autoimmunity a factor that must always be treated
options.why: ASRM asks for TSH and T4 with signs or symptoms and does not recommend autoimmunity screening in asymptomatic women.

options.text: ETA 2021: TSH only and only with symptoms of hypothyroidism, without antibodies, because it does not find TPOAb useful before assisted reproduction
options.why: ETA recommends TSH and TPOAb in every subfertile woman.

options.text: ATA 2026: do not measure TSH in women with infertility unless they have a goitre, because it considers it a low-yield test
options.why: ATA indicates measuring TSH in every non-pregnant woman with infertility (GPS).

options.text: ATA 2026: TSH in every non-pregnant woman with infertility (GPS) and allows TPOAb testing (conditional, low certainty)
options.why: Correct: ETA asks for TSH and TPOAb in all, and ASRM for TSH and T4 with signs or symptoms.

items.explanation: ATA 2026: TSH in every non-pregnant woman with infertility (GPS) and allows TPOAb testing (conditional, low certainty). ETA 2021: TSH and TPOAb in every subfertile woman. ASRM 2024: TSH and T4 with signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism, including irregular cycles, and it does not recommend autoimmunity screening in asymptomatic infertile women.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) wishing to conceive has a TSH of 3.2 mIU/L; her laboratory’s upper limit is 4.5 mIU/L. How does ASRM 2024 classify it?

options.text: As subclinical hypothyroidism, because ASRM sets 2.5 mIU/L as the upper limit for any woman trying to conceive
options.why: ASRM uses the laboratory upper limit or, if none, 4.12 mIU/L.

options.text: It is not subclinical hypothyroidism: it is within her laboratory range, which is the limit ASRM uses
options.why: Correct: only if the laboratory gives no limit is 4.12 mIU/L used.

options.text: As subclinical hypothyroidism, because it exceeds 3.0 mIU/L, ASRM’s fixed threshold regardless of laboratory
options.why: ASRM does not use 3.0 mIU/L as a threshold.

options.text: It cannot be classified without TPOAb, because ASRM defines subclinical hypothyroidism by the presence of antibodies
options.why: The definition rests on TSH relative to the upper limit, not on antibodies.

items.explanation: For ASRM 2024, a TSH of 3.2 within the reference range is not subclinical hypothyroidism: it uses the laboratory upper limit or, if none, 4.12 mIU/L. It also does not recommend levothyroxine even for subclinical hypothyroidism in women desiring pregnancy (evidence B, moderate).

items.stem: A euthyroid woman (fictional case) with positive TPOAb is about to start IVF/ICSI. What does ETA 2021 say?

options.text: It suggests not treating systematically (R19), although it allows case-by-case low-dose levothyroxine with TSH 2.5–4.0 (R15)
options.why: Correct: for R15 it mentions recurrent miscarriage, age > 35 years and ovarian causes of subfertility.

options.text: It recommends full-dose levothyroxine in every TPOAb-positive woman, regardless of TSH, before any ovarian stimulation for IVF
options.why: ETA suggests not treating systematically and only allows low doses case by case.

options.text: It recommends oral prednisolone to lower antibodies before transfer, with a strong recommendation and high certainty
options.why: That position is not in ETA; ATA 2026 advises against prednisolone in women with antibodies and infertility.

options.text: It agrees with ATA 2026 on never offering levothyroxine, whatever the TSH and the patient’s history
options.why: ETA allows low-dose levothyroxine case by case; that is the disagreement with ATA.

items.explanation: ETA 2021 suggests not systematically treating euthyroid women with autoimmunity in IVF/ICSI (R19), but allows low-dose levothyroxine (usually 25–50 µg/day) case by case with autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0 mIU/L before stimulation (R15; 2, ØØOO), mentioning recurrent miscarriage, age > 35 years and ovarian causes of subfertility. ATA 2026 recommends not offering levothyroxine to euthyroid antibody-positive women with infertility (strong, high certainty).

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) with TSH 3.4 mIU/L within range fears her thyroid will cause a miscarriage. What does ASRM 2024 recommend, and what does ATA 2026 rely on?

options.text: ASRM recommends telling her that a TSH of 2.5–4 clearly increases miscarriage risk, and ATA relies on small observational studies
options.why: ASRM advises explaining that it is not associated with more miscarriage, and ATA relies on three high-quality trials.

options.text: ASRM recommends levothyroxine to bring TSH below 2.5, and ATA relies on a meta-analysis showing more live births with treatment
options.why: ASRM does not recommend levothyroxine here, and in the trials ATA cites it did not improve outcomes.

options.text: ASRM recommends counselling that a TSH of 2.5-4 is not associated with more miscarriage (B, moderate); ATA relies on three high-quality randomised trials (refs. 100, 105 and 106: T4LIFE, TABLET and a Chinese IVF trial) with no benefit from levothyroxine
options.why: Correct: these are each guideline’s supports.

options.text: Neither addresses the link between TSH and miscarriage, so there is no basis for reassuring or treating her
options.why: ASRM addresses it expressly with a counselling recommendation.

items.explanation: ASRM 2024 recommends counselling that a TSH between 2.5 and 4 mIU/L is not associated with more miscarriage (evidence B, moderate). ATA 2026 relies on three high-quality randomised trials (guideline refs. 100, 105 and 106: T4LIFE, TABLET and a Chinese IVF trial) in which preconception levothyroxine did not improve fertility or pregnancy outcomes.

items.stem: A euthyroid woman (fictional case) with positive TPOAb is planning a pregnancy. What does ATA 2026 suggest?

options.text: Low-dose levothyroxine while she tries to conceive, because positive antibodies indicate hypothyroidism that has not yet appeared
options.why: Autoimmunity in a euthyroid woman is not an indication for levothyroxine.

options.text: Repeat the antibodies monthly and treat if the titre rises, because the TPOAb titre guides the treatment decision
options.why: ATA suggests monitoring thyroid function (TSH and free T4), not the antibody titre.

options.text: No further monitoring until she is pregnant, because the risk of hypothyroidism appears only during pregnancy
options.why: The 7–9% risk applies before or during pregnancy, and ATA suggests checks while she plans it.

options.text: Recheck TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months while she plans pregnancy (conditional, low certainty)
options.why: Correct: the risk of subclinical hypothyroidism is 7–9%.

items.explanation: According to ATA 2026, TPOAb positivity is associated with a 7–9% risk of developing subclinical hypothyroidism before or during pregnancy, and autoimmunity in a euthyroid woman is not an indication for levothyroxine; it therefore suggests rechecking TSH and free T4 every 3–6 months while she plans pregnancy (conditional, low certainty).

items.stem: A euthyroid TPOAb-positive woman with infertility (fictional case) asks about prednisolone, intravenous immunoglobulin or selenium. What does ATA 2026 say?

options.text: It recommends selenium for all to lower antibodies before pregnancy, and reserves prednisolone for those with very high titres
options.why: ATA advises against selenium in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women and does not offer prednisolone.

options.text: Do not offer oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin (conditional, low), and it advises against selenium in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate)
options.why: Correct: these are ATA’s positions.

options.text: Offer intravenous immunoglobulin if she has had previous miscarriages, because in that subgroup ATA recommends it with high certainty
options.why: ATA does not offer intravenous immunoglobulin in these women.

options.text: It takes no position on any of these treatments, because it considers them outside the scope of a thyroid guideline
options.why: ATA expressly addresses all three.

items.explanation: ATA 2026 states that oral prednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin should not be offered to women with TPOAb and/or TgAb and infertility (conditional, low certainty) and advises against selenium supplements in euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate certainty).

items.stem: During follow-up, a TPOAb-positive woman trying to conceive (fictional case) develops hypothyroidism and needs levothyroxine. What TSH target does ATA 2026 give for women with infertility?

options.text: 0.5–2.5 mIU/L before and during pregnancy (GPS)
options.why: Correct: this is the target ATA gives.

options.text: Below 1.0 mIU/L, because in antibody-positive women TSH should be kept as low as possible to protect implantation
options.why: ATA gives 0.5–2.5 mIU/L; it does not propose suppressing TSH.

options.text: Any value below 4.12 mIU/L, the upper limit ATA uses for all women trying to conceive
options.why: 4.12 mIU/L is the limit ASRM uses when the laboratory gives none; it is not ATA’s treatment target.

options.text: None in particular: ATA leaves the target to clinical judgement, because it considers there are no data to set a range in these patients
options.why: ATA sets a target (GPS).

items.explanation: If a woman with infertility needs levothyroxine, ATA 2026 sets a TSH target of 0.5–2.5 mIU/L before and during pregnancy (GPS). Isolated autoimmunity in a euthyroid woman is not an indication to treat.

items.stem: A woman with PCOS (fictional case), not currently seeking pregnancy, asks about inositol “for metabolism”. What does the 2023 PCOS guideline say in this general setting?

options.text: That it is recommended as first-line treatment of PCOS, with moderate certainty, because of its proven effect on weight
options.why: The guideline notes limited clinical benefit, including on weight, and very low certainty.

options.text: That it is contraindicated, because the guideline has documented serious adverse effects and advises against any form of inositol
options.why: The guideline does not contraindicate it: in the general setting it notes limited harm and limited clinical benefit (4.7.1); only in the infertility section does it add that side effects and safety are not known (5.8.3).

options.text: That it could be considered based on preferences and values, with limited harm, potential metabolic improvement and limited clinical benefit (conditional, very low certainty)
options.why: Correct: different from its use as a fertility treatment, which the guideline considers experimental.

options.text: That only the 40:1 myo-inositol to D-chiro-inositol combination may be used, the only one the guideline recommends
options.why: The guideline says no specific type, dose or combination can be recommended.

items.explanation: The 2023 PCOS guideline says that inositol, in any form, could be considered based on preferences and values, noting limited harm, potential metabolic improvement and limited clinical benefit, including in ovulation, hirsutism or weight (conditional, very low certainty). In women with PCOS and infertility, by contrast, it should be considered experimental therapy.

items.stem: An anovulatory woman with PCOS (fictional case), with no other infertility factors, wants treatment to ovulate. Under the 2023 PCOS guideline, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Inositol for at least six months, moving to letrozole only if she does not ovulate, to avoid drugs with side effects
options.why: Inositol as a fertility treatment is experimental and should not delay letrozole.

options.text: Letrozole (strong, high certainty), together with lifestyle intervention for metabolic health
options.why: Correct: lifestyle is recommended for all (strong, very low certainty).

options.text: Gonadotrophins from the first cycle, because the guideline considers oral drugs no longer have a role in PCOS
options.why: The guideline places letrozole as the first-line pharmacological treatment.

options.text: Low-dose levothyroxine if TSH exceeds 2.5 mIU/L, because it corrects PCOS anovulation in most women
options.why: The guideline does not propose levothyroxine for PCOS anovulation.

items.explanation: For ovulation induction in anovulatory women with PCOS and no other infertility factors, the first-line pharmacological treatment is letrozole (strong, high certainty), and lifestyle intervention is recommended for all to improve metabolic health (strong, very low certainty). If she wants inositol, it should be an informed choice that does not delay letrozole.

items.stem: A patient (fictional case) shows three inositol products with different ratios and doses and asks which is best. What do the 2023 PCOS guideline practice points say?

options.text: That the highest-dose product is preferred, because the guideline has shown a clear dose-response effect on ovulation
options.why: The guideline recommends no specific dose and describes no such gradient.

options.text: That all are equivalent, because they are made to pharmaceutical standards and the guideline considers their regulation strict and uniform in every country
options.why: The guideline warns that these products may have limited regulation.

options.text: That the one containing only D-chiro-inositol should be chosen, because the guideline advises against myo-inositol in PCOS
options.why: The guideline prefers no form and does not advise against myo-inositol.

options.text: That no specific type, dose or combination can be recommended, that side effects and safety are unknown, and that regulation may be limited
options.why: Correct: these are the practice points.

items.explanation: The 2023 PCOS guideline notes that no specific type, dose or combination of inositol can be recommended, that its side effects and safety are not known, and that these products may have limited regulation, with variable dose, quality and combinations (practice points).

items.stem: What does USPSTF (grade A) recommend about folic acid for people who plan to or could become pregnant?

options.text: A daily supplement of 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy
options.why: Correct: this is the USPSTF recommendation.

options.text: A 4 mg daily supplement for everyone, from the day of the positive pregnancy test until the end of the second trimester of pregnancy
options.why: The USPSTF dose is 0.4–0.8 mg and starts before conception.

options.text: No supplement if the diet is varied, because USPSTF considers dietary folate sufficient for most women
options.why: USPSTF recommends the supplement for everyone who plans to or could become pregnant.

options.text: A 0.4 mg supplement only in women with PCOS and BMI > 30 kg/m², since in others the neural tube defect risk is minimal
options.why: USPSTF does not restrict the recommendation; it is the PCOS guideline that mentions a higher dose with BMI > 30, without specifying it.

items.explanation: USPSTF recommends (grade A) that everyone who plans to or could become pregnant take a daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, from at least 1 month before conception through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. The PCOS guideline includes folate in preconception care, with a higher dose if BMI is > 30 kg/m² (without specifying it).

items.stem: Numerical exercise: a pregnant woman (fictional case) takes a prenatal multivitamin with 150 µg of iodine and, on her own initiative, a seaweed supplement with 400 µg. What is the total, and what does ATA 2026 say?

options.text: 250 µg/day, exactly ATA’s target, because seaweed iodine is not absorbed and only the multivitamin counts
options.why: The supplement total is 150 + 400 = 550 µg; ATA makes no such absorption distinction.

options.text: 400 µg/day, because only the highest-dose supplement counts, and that figure is below ATA’s limit
options.why: The iodine from all supplements must be added.

options.text: 550 µg/day from supplements, above the 500 µg/day that ATA asks to avoid in pregnancy (strong, moderate)
550 µg/day, an amount ATA recommends for vegan pregnant women to make up for the lack of iodised salt
options.why: For women at risk of deficiency, ATA suggests 150 µg/day, and asks to avoid supplements > 500 µg/day.

items.explanation: 150 + 400 = 550 µg/day of iodine from supplements (check: 550 − 500 = 50 µg above the limit). ATA 2026 asks to avoid sustained excessive iodine intake and supplements above 500 µg/day in pregnancy because of concerns for fetal and maternal thyroid dysfunction (strong, moderate); it recommends that pregnant and lactating women aim for a daily intake of 250 µg from diet plus supplements (strong, moderate).

items.stem: A woman with PCOS (fictional case) is about to start ovulation induction with letrozole. What do the 2023 PCOS guideline and ATA 2026 ask regarding supplements?

options.text: Delay any prenatal vitamin until pregnancy is confirmed, because supplements interfere with the letrozole response
options.why: The PCOS guideline asks for prenatal vitamins to start together with ovulation induction.

options.text: Start prenatal supplementation together with ovulation induction; ATA suggests 150 µg/day of iodine if she is at risk of deficiency, ideally from at least 3 months before
options.why: Correct: PCOS guideline practice point and ATA conditional, moderate recommendation.

options.text: Take 1000 µg of iodine daily from the start of induction, which ATA recommends for all women with PCOS because of their higher thyroid risk
options.why: ATA asks to avoid supplements > 500 µg/day in pregnancy and makes no PCOS-specific recommendation.

options.text: Replace folic acid with inositol, because the PCOS guideline considers that inositol also covers neural tube defect prevention
options.why: The guideline makes no such claim; it includes folate in preconception care.

items.explanation: The 2023 PCOS guideline includes folate in preconception care (higher dose with BMI > 30 kg/m², unspecified) and asks for prenatal supplementation to start together with ovulation induction (consensus and practice point). ATA 2026 suggests a 150 µg/day iodine supplement, ideally from at least 3 months before pregnancy until lactation is complete, in women at risk of deficiency because of region, diet or malabsorption (conditional, moderate).

items.stem: A woman with endometriosis (fictional case) is offered 3 months of GnRH agonist before IVF “to improve pregnancy rates”. What does ESHRE 2022 say?

options.text: It recommends it for every woman with endometriosis before IVF, because it improves live births with moderate certainty
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend extended agonist administration before assisted reproduction.

options.text: It recommends it only with an endometrioma over 3 cm, as an alternative to surgery to preserve ovarian reserve
options.why: The guideline sets no such indication or threshold.

options.text: It takes no position on hormonal suppression before IVF, because it considers it a decision for the IVF laboratory
options.why: ESHRE takes an explicit position with strong recommendations.

options.text: It does not recommend extended GnRH agonist administration before assisted reproduction (strong, ⊕) or ovarian suppression to improve fertility (strong, ⊕⊕)
options.why: Correct: these are two strong recommendations of the guideline.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2022 does not recommend ovarian suppression to improve fertility (strong, ⊕⊕) or extended GnRH agonist administration before assisted reproduction (strong, ⊕). Nor does it recommend routine endometrioma surgery before assisted reproduction to improve live birth (strong, ⊕⊕).

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman (fictional case) with an endometrioma and infertility prefers to try for a spontaneous pregnancy before IVF. What do ESHRE 2022 and NICE NG73 say?

options.text: ESHRE says operative laparoscopy may be considered (weak, ⊕), with caution to minimise ovarian damage; NICE offers cystectomy or drainage and ablation, considering ovarian reserve
options.why: Correct: and NICE advises against hormonal treatment for people trying to conceive (1.10.4).

options.text: Both recommend 6 months of suppressive hormonal treatment before trying for a spontaneous pregnancy, to shrink the endometrioma
options.why: NICE advises against hormonal treatment, alone or with surgery, for people trying to conceive, and ESHRE does not recommend suppression to improve fertility.

options.text: ESHRE strongly recommends surgery based on several comparative studies, and NICE advises against it in any circumstance
options.why: ESHRE’s recommendation is weak and no comparative studies exist; NICE offers surgery.

options.text: Neither considers surgery if the patient will not have IVF, because both reserve endometrioma management for assisted reproduction
options.why: Both consider surgery in this situation.

items.explanation: If the couple prefers to try for a spontaneous pregnancy, ESHRE 2022 says operative laparoscopy may be considered for endometrioma-associated infertility, although no comparative studies exist (weak, ⊕), with specific caution to minimise ovarian damage (strong, ⊕). NICE NG73 offers cystectomy or drainage and ablation, taking into account the possible impact on ovarian reserve (1.10.2), and advises against hormonal treatment, alone or with surgery, for people trying to conceive (1.10.4).

items.stem: What do the WHO 2021 semen reference limits mean, such as a concentration of 16 × 10⁶/ml and 30% progressive motility?

options.text: They are the minimum values below which a man is sterile, so any lower result confirms infertility
options.why: Semen analysis cannot precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men, except in azoospermia and some extreme pictures.

options.text: They are the median for men in the general population, so half of fertile men have values below them
options.why: They are the 5th centile, not the median, and come from men whose partners conceived within 12 months.

options.text: They are the 5th centile of men whose partners conceived within 12 months, and AUA/ASRM notes that semen analysis cannot precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men
options.why: Correct: a value just below is a finding to confirm.

options.text: They are the targets an antioxidant treatment should reach, which AUA/ASRM strongly recommends until they normalise
options.why: AUA/ASRM considers antioxidants and vitamins of questionable clinical utility.

items.explanation: The WHO 2021 reference limits are the 5th centile of men whose partners conceived within 12 months (for example, concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml and progressive motility 30%). AUA/ASRM points out that semen analysis cannot precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men except in azoospermia and some extreme pictures.

items.stem: A man (fictional case) has two abnormal semen analyses 3 months apart. What does NICE NG257 offer next?

options.text: A third semen analysis at 3 months before any examination, because NICE requires three abnormal results before investigating the man
options.why: With 2 or more abnormal analyses, NICE already offers examination.

options.text: Examination of the scrotum and testes, and consider measuring testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5)
options.why: Correct: this is what NICE indicates with 2 or more abnormal analyses.

options.text: Routine sperm DNA fragmentation testing, which NICE recommends as the next step for any semen abnormality
options.why: NICE advises against sperm DNA fragmentation testing (1.17.6).

options.text: ICSI straight away without further work-up, because NICE indicates it for any abnormal semen analysis regardless of severity
options.why: NICE suggests considering ICSI taking severity into account, and also offers examination.

items.explanation: With 2 or more abnormal analyses, NICE NG257 offers examination of the scrotum and testes and suggests considering testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5); it advises against sperm DNA fragmentation testing (1.17.6).

items.stem: A man’s (fictional case) first semen analysis shows azoospermia. According to NICE NG257, when is it repeated?

options.text: At 3 months, like any other abnormal result, to allow the sperm formation cycle to be completed
options.why: 3 months is for non-severe abnormalities; in azoospermia it is repeated as soon as possible.

options.text: At 12 months, because azoospermia usually resolves spontaneously and repeating sooner only causes anxiety
options.why: NICE indicates repeating it as soon as possible.

options.text: It is not repeated, because a single azoospermic analysis is diagnostic and AUA/ASRM advises against repeating it
options.why: NICE offers a repeat as soon as possible, and AUA/ASRM includes one or more semen analyses in the initial evaluation.

options.text: As soon as possible (1.17.4), unlike non-severe abnormalities, which are ideally repeated at 3 months
options.why: Correct: as in severe oligozoospermia.

items.explanation: NICE NG257 offers a repeat abnormal semen analysis ideally at 3 months to allow the sperm formation cycle to be completed, except in azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, when it is repeated as soon as possible (1.17.3–1.17.4). AUA/ASRM recommends assessing both partners concurrently (expert opinion) and including one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (strong; evidence B).

items.stem: According to ESHRE 2022, in which situations can assisted reproduction especially be used for endometriosis-associated infertility?

options.text: Only after surgery has failed, because the guideline always requires an operation before any assisted reproduction technique
options.why: The guideline does not require prior surgery and does not recommend routine endometrioma surgery before assisted reproduction.

options.text: Only in deep endometriosis with bowel involvement, because in peritoneal endometriosis the guideline advises against it
options.why: The guideline does not restrict it to deep endometriosis.

options.text: If tubal function is compromised, there is male factor, the EFI is low or other treatments have failed (weak, ⊕⊕)
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE’s recommendation.

options.text: In any woman with endometriosis under 35, regardless of tubes, semen or EFI
options.why: The guideline uses no such age criterion; it lists specific situations.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2022 states that assisted reproduction can be used for endometriosis-associated infertility, especially if tubal function is compromised, there is male factor, the EFI is low or other treatments have failed (weak, ⊕⊕). It does not recommend a specific protocol: GnRH antagonist or agonist according to preferences (weak, ⊕).

items.stem: A couple (fictional case) with endometriosis and normal semen is starting IVF. Which statement about protocol, ICSI and supplements is correct?

options.text: Antagonist or agonist according to preferences (weak, ⊕); ESHRE does not recommend ICSI without male factor; AUA/ASRM considers antioxidants of questionable utility
options.why: Correct: it summarises the three positions.

options.text: A mandatory long agonist protocol because of the endometriosis, and ICSI always to compensate for these women’s poorer oocyte quality
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend a specific protocol and does not recommend ICSI without male factor.

options.text: A mandatory antagonist protocol for its higher live birth rate in endometriosis, and ICSI recommended by NICE in all IVF
options.why: No difference between protocols has been shown, and NICE reserves ICSI for abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation.

options.text: Any protocol, ICSI by couple preference and antioxidants for the man, which AUA/ASRM recommends with grade A
options.why: AUA/ASRM considers supplements of questionable clinical utility (moderate; grade B), and ICSI without male factor is not recommended.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2022 does not recommend a specific protocol (antagonist or agonist according to preferences; weak, ⊕). The ESHRE add-ons document does not recommend ICSI without male factor, and NICE reserves it for abnormal semen by severity or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2). AUA/ASRM considers antioxidants and vitamins of questionable clinical utility, with no data to recommend specific agents (moderate; grade B).

items.stem: On PGT-A and endometrial scratching, what do ESHRE 2023 and NICE NG257 say?

options.text: ESHRE recommends them in women over 38, and NICE offers them after two failed transfers
options.why: ESHRE rates them “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”, and NICE advises not offering them.

options.text: ESHRE considers them “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”; NICE advises not offering PGT-A to improve live birth or scratching as pre-treatment
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.48.1 and 1.40.1.

options.text: ESHRE classifies them as “not recommended” for lack of biological rationale, like peripheral blood immune tests
options.why: Immune tests are “not recommended”; PGT-A and scratching are “currently not recommended for routine use”.

options.text: NICE does not address them, so in the UK they are left to each clinic’s discretion without any guidance
options.why: NICE addresses them expressly, advising not to offer them.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2023 considers PGT-A and endometrial scratching “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (may change with more evidence), and does not recommend receptivity tests or immune tests. NICE NG257 advises not offering receptivity testing (1.41.1), PGT-A to improve live birth (1.48.1) or scratching as pre-treatment (1.40.1).

items.stem: In the same extras package, the clinic offers the man sperm DNA fragmentation testing and antioxidants. What do ESHRE 2023 and NICE NG257 say?

options.text: Both recommend both, because high fragmentation justifies antioxidants to improve IVF live births
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction and NICE advises against the test.

options.text: NICE recommends fragmentation testing for all couples before IVF, and ESHRE recommends antioxidants if it is abnormal
options.why: It reverses the positions: NICE advises against the test and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants.

options.text: ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction, and NICE advises against sperm DNA fragmentation testing (1.17.6)
options.why: Correct: neither male extra has support.

options.text: Neither takes a position on male extras, because both guidelines deal only with interventions on the woman, the embryo and the laboratory
options.why: Both take a position on these two male extras.

items.explanation: For the man, ESHRE 2023 does not recommend antioxidants in assisted reproduction, and NICE NG257 advises against sperm DNA fragmentation testing (1.17.6). Among the extras in this package, the only one ESHRE recommends is hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium, with a single embryo transfer policy (artificial oocyte and sperm activation are also recommended, but only for very specific indications).

items.stem: What does the 2023 ESHRE add-ons guideline ask regarding how these interventions should be offered in clinical practice?

options.text: That each test or intervention be evaluated for efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness, that this be part of counselling and that only evidence-based add-ons be offered
options.why: Correct: these are the guideline’s general requests.

options.text: That all available extras be offered and the couple choose freely, because the guideline considers autonomy to prevail over evidence
