options.why: The guideline asks for only evidence-based add-ons to be offered.

options.text: That only add-ons with high-quality evidence be offered, which according to the guideline are most of its 42 recommendations
options.why: None of the 42 recommendations rests on high-quality evidence.

options.text: That cost not be taken into account, because the guideline considers price not part of the clinical decision on an add-on
options.why: The guideline includes cost-effectiveness among the evaluation criteria.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2023 asks for every test or intervention to be evaluated for efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness, for this evaluation to become a standard part of counselling, and for only evidence-based add-ons to be offered in clinical practice; of its 42 recommendations, none rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman (fictional case) has had no periods for 6 months and has hot flushes. How does she fit under ESHRE 2024 and NICE NG23?

options.text: It is premature ovarian insufficiency, because ESHRE 2024 defines it as loss of ovarian activity before age 45
options.why: ESHRE defines POI before age 40; between 40 and 44 it is early menopause.

options.text: Perimenopause can be diagnosed without tests, because NICE allows this from age 40 with symptoms
options.why: NICE identifies perimenopause without tests from age 45.

options.text: AMH should be ordered to confirm menopause, which NICE prefers to FSH in women aged 40 to 45
options.why: NICE proposes considering FSH between 40 and 45; it advises against AMH from age 45.

options.text: It is not POI (before 40): 40–44 is early menopause, outside ESHRE’s scope; NICE proposes considering FSH
options.why: Correct: always also considering other causes of the cycle change.

items.explanation: ESHRE 2024 defines premature ovarian insufficiency as loss of ovarian activity before age 40; it calls cessation between 40 and 44 early menopause, outside its scope. NICE identifies perimenopause without tests from age 45 and, between 40 and 45 with symptoms, proposes considering FSH to confirm menopause (1.3.6).

items.stem: A 43-year-old woman (fictional case) on a combined hormonal contraceptive asks for an FSH “to know whether she is in menopause”. What does NICE NG23 say?

options.text: That FSH is reliable with any hormonal contraception and a single measurement is enough to confirm menopause
options.why: NICE advises against using FSH in people on combined hormonal contraception or high-dose progestogen.

options.text: That FSH should not be used to identify menopause in people using combined hormonal contraception or high-dose progestogen (1.3.5)
options.why: Correct: the contraceptive distorts interpretation.

options.text: That FSH should be replaced by AMH, which NICE recommends in these women because contraceptives do not affect it
options.why: NICE does not propose AMH to identify menopause and advises against it from age 45.

options.text: That FSH should be measured together with estradiol and inhibin, because NICE recommends that full panel for all women aged 40 to 45
options.why: NICE proposes no such panel, and advises against estradiol and inhibins from age 45.

items.explanation: NICE NG23 advises against using FSH to identify menopause in people using combined hormonal contraception or high-dose progestogen (1.3.5), and from age 45 against AMH, inhibins, estradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume (1.3.4). With a cycle change, other causes such as hyperprolactinaemia should also be considered.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) on an antipsychotic has a prolactin 3 times the upper limit, but reports new headache and visual disturbance. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society indicate?

options.text: Repeat prolactin only, because below 5 times the upper limit MRI is not indicated even with symptoms
options.why: Repetition applies to an isolated elevation; mass symptoms indicate MRI.

options.text: Attribute it to the antipsychotic and wait, because headache is a common side effect of these drugs
options.why: With mass symptoms, the consensus indicates MRI.

options.text: Pituitary MRI, because mass symptoms such as headache or visual disturbance are an indication even if prolactin does not exceed 10 times the limit
options.why: Correct: as are prolactin > 10 times the limit or non-gonadal pituitary deficits.

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic yourself and repeat prolactin 48 hours later, to clarify whether the cause is the drug before ordering any kind of pituitary imaging
options.why: You should not stop the antipsychotic yourself: any change is coordinated with psychiatry, and mass symptoms indicate MRI.

items.explanation: In people on antipsychotics, the 2023 Pituitary Society indicates MRI if prolactin exceeds 10 times the upper limit, there are mass-effect symptoms such as headache or visual disturbance, or there are pituitary deficiencies other than the gonadal axis. Management requires collaboration between endocrinology, neurosurgery and psychiatry (strong).

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman (fictional case) on an antipsychotic for years has a prolactin 14 times the upper limit, with no mass symptoms. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society indicate?

options.text: Suspect a prolactinoma and order MRI, because elevations described with antipsychotics reach up to 10 times the limit
options.why: Correct: this is the consensus threshold (strong).

options.text: Attribute it to the antipsychotic, because after years of treatment any elevation is drug-induced, whatever its size
options.why: Above 10 times the limit, prolactinoma should be suspected.

options.text: Repeat prolactin, because any value must be repeated before MRI, just like values below 5 times the limit
options.why: Repetition is recommended with values < 5 times the limit; with > 10 times MRI is indicated.

options.text: Start cabergoline without imaging and assess response, because MRI is indicated only with headache or visual disturbance
options.why: Prolactin > 10 times the limit is in itself an indication for MRI.

items.explanation: Hyperprolactinaemia occurs in 30–75% of people on antipsychotics within the first 3 months, with elevations of up to 10 times the upper limit described; above 10 times, a prolactinoma should be suspected (strong), and MRI is indicated. Values < 5 times the limit should be repeated (strong).

items.stem: According to NAMS 2022, which of these hormones are approved, regulated bioidentical hormones?

options.text: Subdermal testosterone and estradiol pellets, which NAMS considers the reference regulated bioidentical format
options.why: Pellets and implants are examples of untested routes for compounded preparations.

options.text: Estradiol, estrone and micronized progesterone
options.why: Correct: these are the approved bioidenticals NAMS lists.

options.text: Sublingual troches with several combined hormones, because they are tailored to each woman’s needs
options.why: Troches are an example of compounded products with untested combinations or routes.

options.text: Any pharmacy preparation made from plants, because “bioidentical” means of natural origin
options.why: NAMS warns that the term can mislead; what matters is whether it is approved and regulated.

items.explanation: NAMS 2022 warns that “bioidentical” can mislead: there are approved, regulated bioidentical hormones (estradiol, estrone and micronized progesterone) and compounded preparations that may combine several hormones in untested combinations, formulations or routes, such as subdermal implants, pellets or troches.

items.stem: Which safety concerns does NAMS 2022 attribute to compounded hormone preparations (Level I)?

options.text: None, provided the pharmacy is licensed, because compounding guarantees the same quality as an approved medicine
options.why: NAMS describes minimal regulation and monitoring and lack of efficacy and safety data.

options.text: Only a higher price, because NAMS acknowledges their efficacy and safety are shown in trials equivalent to approved ones
options.why: NAMS notes a lack of efficacy and safety data.

options.text: Only the risk of underdosing, because pharmacies tend to use lower doses than approved products
options.why: NAMS mentions both overdosing and underdosing, among other problems.

options.text: Minimal regulation and monitoring, over- and underdosing, impurities and lack of sterility, lack of efficacy and safety data, and no label outlining risks
options.why: Correct: this is the NAMS list (Level I).

items.explanation: NAMS 2022 attributes to compounded preparations minimal regulation and monitoring, overdosing and underdosing, impurities and lack of sterility, lack of efficacy and safety data, and no label outlining risks (Level I). Patient preference alone does not justify a compounded preparation, particularly when regulated bioidentical hormones are available (Level III).

items.stem: Before a stool microbiome test her doctor ordered (fictional case), a patient asks whether she should stop her medication and change her diet “for a cleaner result”. What does the 2025 international consensus say?

options.text: That she must stop all medication at least two weeks before, because drugs invalidate any microbiome profile
options.why: The consensus says she should not suspend her therapy unless the referring physician recommends it.

options.text: That she must follow the laboratory’s standard diet for a month, because the consensus requires a common diet to compare results
options.why: The consensus says not to change diet before the test unless the referring physician recommends it.

options.text: That she should not suspend her therapy or change her diet before testing unless the referring physician recommends it (100%)
options.why: Correct: a statement with unanimous agreement.

options.text: That she should take a probiotic for a week beforehand, because the report then better reflects her “baseline” microbiota
options.why: The consensus proposes no such preparation.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus states that patients should not suspend their therapy or change their diet before testing unless the referring physician recommends it (100%), and that any change in management should be made only by the referring professional (100%). It also considers the evidence insufficient to widely recommend routine use (90%).

items.stem: A patient (fictional case) asks whether she can order a gut microbiome test online, without consulting anyone, “to know herself better”. What does the 2025 international consensus say?

options.text: That it discourages patients from requesting these tests directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%)
options.why: Correct: moreover, any change in management belongs to the referring professional.

options.text: That it recommends it for the whole healthy population as annual screening, because it detects dysbiosis before symptoms appear
options.why: The consensus considers the evidence insufficient for routine use and finds no basis for dysbiosis indices.

options.text: That it accepts it provided the report includes a personalised supplement plan prepared by the laboratory itself
options.why: The consensus discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice (98%).

options.text: That it takes no position on direct-to-consumer tests, because it only assesses hospital-based tests
options.why: The consensus takes an explicit position and warns of their proliferation without proven clinical value.

items.explanation: The 2025 consensus (69 experts, Delphi) discourages patients from requesting these tests directly without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), considers the evidence insufficient to widely recommend routine use (90%) and discourages the provider from including therapeutic advice (98%).

items.stem: According to NAMS 2022, in which women is the benefit–risk balance of hormone therapy most favourable?

options.text: In women over 65 with more than 15 years since menopause, because their baseline fracture risk is higher
options.why: NAMS places the most favourable balance before 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset.

options.text: In women who start it before 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, without contraindications
options.why: Correct: this is the window NAMS describes.

options.text: In any symptomatic woman, regardless of age or time since menopause, because the balance does not depend on timing
options.why: NAMS describes a timing window; timing does matter.

options.text: Only in women with surgical menopause, because in natural menopause the balance is always unfavourable
options.why: NAMS does not restrict the favourable balance to surgical menopause.

items.explanation: NAMS 2022 places the most favourable balance of hormone therapy in women who start it before 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, without contraindications, and considers absolute risk more useful than relative risk for conveying benefits and risks.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman (fictional case) with troublesome hot flushes does not want to take hormones. Besides discussing all options, what does NICE propose?

options.text: Insist on HRT as the only effective option, because NICE considers that declining hormones is not a valid preference
options.why: NICE asks you to accept that the person may weigh risks and benefits differently and offers alternatives.

options.text: Offer compounded hormone preparations, which NICE recommends as a “natural” alternative for those who do not want conventional hormones
options.why: NICE does not recommend them, and NAMS describes their safety concerns.

options.text: Consider menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy as an option, including when she prefers not to take hormones
options.why: Correct: alongside discussing all options, including no treatment.

options.text: Offer no alternative, because without hormones NICE considers hot flushes to have no effective treatment
options.why: NICE proposes considering menopause-specific CBT.

items.explanation: For vasomotor symptoms, NICE NG23 recommends offering HRT and considering menopause-specific cognitive behavioural therapy as an option, including when the person prefers not to take hormones. NICE NG197 asks for the risks, benefits and consequences of each option to be discussed, including no treatment or no change, and for the person’s different weighing to be accepted.

asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism in the infertile female population: a guideline
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.population: Women with infertility or miscarriage and pregnant women, in relation to subclinical hypothyroidism. Replaces the 2015 ASRM version.
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.finding: Use the laboratory TSH cut-offs; if unavailable, 4.12 mIU/L for non-pregnant women and those attempting pregnancy (B; moderate). Counsel that subclinical hypothyroidism and a TSH of 2.5–4.0 mIU/L are not associated with more miscarriage (B; moderate). Treating subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in women desiring pregnancy or pregnant is not recommended (B; moderate). Test TSH and T4 when there are signs or symptoms of hypothyroidism (including irregular cycles), not in all infertility patients (B; moderate). Do not screen asymptomatic women for thyroid autoimmunity; it may be considered in recurrent pregnancy loss (C; weak).
asrm-2024-subclinical-hypothyroidism.limitations: Full PDF read (Fertil Steril 2024;121:765-82). Strength of evidence A/B/C and strength of recommendation strong/moderate/weak. Much of its position rests on an influential trial having data-integrity concerns. US context.

ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.title: American Thyroid Association 2026 Guidelines for Thyroid Disease in Preconception, Pregnancy, and Postpartum
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.authors: Korevaar TIM, Leung AM, Alexander EK, Bliddal S, Boelaert K, Brenta G, Chou R, Dhillon-Smith R, Dosiou C, Eaton JL, Guan H, Kilpatrick SJ, Lasserre BJ, Lee SY, Maraka S, Meister KD, Morris-Wiseman LF, Nguyen CT, Pearce EN, Shan Z
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.population: Women planning pregnancy (including those with infertility, recurrent miscarriage or fertility treatment), pregnant women and women postpartum or breastfeeding. Replaces the 2017 ATA guideline; endorsed by, among others, ESHRE, the European Thyroid Association, ACOG, the Endocrine Society and the Latin American Thyroid Society.
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.finding: Infertility: TSH for all women with infertility or recurrent miscarriage (GPS) and optional TPOAb (conditional, low); on levothyroxine, target TSH 0.5–2.5 mU/L (GPS). Subclinical hypothyroidism: confirm after 4–6 weeks (conditional, moderate); TSH > 10 mU/L, treat (GPS); if persistent, low-dose levothyroxine (25–75 mcg/day; 25–50 in flowchart 1) (conditional, low certainty). Euthyroid autoimmunity (TPOAb and/or TgAb): do not offer levothyroxine (strong, high), recheck TSH and FT4 every 3–6 months; no prednisolone or immunoglobulin. Pregnancy: without a laboratory-specific interval, TSH 0.1–4.0 mU/L in the first and second trimesters. Iodine: 250 mcg/day total intake in pregnancy and lactation (strong, moderate); 150 mcg/day supplement in women at risk of deficiency (conditional, moderate); avoid > 500 mcg/day. Do not offer selenium to euthyroid antibody-positive pregnant women (conditional, moderate).
ata-2026-thyroid-pregnancy.limitations: Full text read in the published version deposited in the University of California repository (eScholarship). Recommendations carry no individual number: they are cited by their “Recommendations Table” and page. Strength strong (“should”) or conditional (“may”), GRADE certainty very low to high, or good practice statement (GPS). The authors acknowledge that much of the evidence is of low or moderate quality; dissenting comments from group members are in supplementary material that was not reviewed. It gives no data specific to Argentina or Spain.

aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline (2020; amended 2024)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.authors: American Urological Association; American Society for Reproductive Medicine (Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.population: Male partners of couples with infertility.
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.finding: Statement 1: concurrent assessment of both partners in the initial evaluation (Expert Opinion). Statement 2: reproductive history (Clinical Principle) and one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level Grade B). Statement 7: advise couples with advanced paternal age (≥40) of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes for offspring (Expert Opinion).
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.limitations: Official AUA page read: summary of all guideline statements and discussion on semen analysis, hormones, DNA fragmentation, pregnancy loss, imaging, varicocele, testosterone and supplements. Statement numbers do not always appear in the extracted text; Part I/II DOIs not verified. US context.

eshre-2022-endometriosis.title: ESHRE guideline: endometriosis (full guideline)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.authors: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline Development Group (Becker CM, Bokor A, Heikinheimo O, Horne A, Jansen F, Kiesel L, King K, Kvaskoff M, Nap A, Petersen K, et al.)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.population: Women with diagnosed or strongly suspected endometriosis; includes chapters on pain, infertility, recurrence, adolescence and menopause. Does not cover adenomyosis. Literature search up to 1 Dec 2020. Full 192-page guideline; recommendations labelled strong or weak (GRADE) with their level of evidence (⊕ symbols), plus good practice points (GPP) and guideline group (GDG) statements.
eshre-2022-endometriosis.finding: Diagnosis: use imaging (ultrasound or MRI), aware that a negative result does not exclude it, particularly superficial peritoneal disease (rec. 5, strong, ⊕⊕); do not use biomarkers (rec. 4, strong, ⊕⊕⊕); diagnostic laparoscopy or imaging plus empirical treatment, with no proven superiority of either (GDG statement); empirical treatment is considered if the patient is not trying to conceive. Infertility: do not prescribe ovarian suppression to improve fertility (rec. 39, strong, ⊕⊕) or postoperative suppression solely to enhance pregnancy rates (rec. 40, strong, ⊕⊕); operative laparoscopy in rASRM stage I/II (rec. 43, weak, ⊕⊕); for endometrioma (rec. 44, weak, ⊕) and deep disease (rec. 45, weak, ⊕); use the EFI to identify who benefits from ART after surgery (GDG statement); IUI with ovarian stimulation in stage I/II (rec. 47, weak, ⊕); ART if tubal or male factor, low EFI or failed other treatments (rec. 49, weak, ⊕⊕); no preferred protocol (rec. 50, weak, ⊕); no extended GnRH agonist before ART (rec. 53, strong, ⊕); insufficient evidence for COC/progestogen pre-treatment (rec. 54, weak, ⊕); no routine surgery before ART in stage I/II (rec. 55, strong, ⊕⊕) or for endometrioma (rec. 56, strong, ⊕⊕); endometrioma surgery before ART for pain or follicle access (rec. 57, GPP); fertility preservation: discuss pros and cons with extensive ovarian endometriosis (rec. 59, strong, ⊕); no non-medical intervention (nutrition, Chinese medicine, acupuncture, etc.) can be recommended to increase fertility (GDG statement).
eshre-2022-endometriosis.limitations: Read in the full guideline: the list of recommendations (pp. 9–14), sections I.2.b–I.2.c, II.3.e (ovarian reserve) and III.1–III.8. The guideline produced no GRADE summary-of-findings tables because evidence was insufficient; most infertility recommendations rest on ⊕ or ⊕⊕ evidence and several are GPPs (expert opinion). Level of evidence per Annex 4: ⊕ very low, ⊕⊕ low, ⊕⊕⊕ moderate, ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high; a recommendation can be strong with ⊕ evidence. Surgical studies were not stratified by EFI. Search closed in 2020; whether a later update exists was not checked.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2024-poi.title: Evidence-based guideline: premature ovarian insufficiency
eshre-2024-poi.authors: POI Guideline Group (ESHRE, ASRM, CRE-WHiRL, IMS); Panay N, Anderson RA, Bennie A, Cedars M, Davies M, Ee C, Gravholt CH, Kalantaridou S, Kallen A, Kim KQ, Misrahi M, Mousa A, Nappi RE, Rocca WA, Ruan X, Teede H, Vermeulen N, Vogt E, Vincent AJ
eshre-2024-poi.population: Women with premature ovarian insufficiency (loss of ovarian activity before age 40), spontaneous or iatrogenic, and their relatives. 2024 update of the 2015/2016 ESHRE guideline, developed with ASRM, CRE-WHiRL and IMS; co-published in Human Reproduction Open, Fertility and Sterility and Climacteric. It does not apply to low ovarian reserve.
eshre-2024-poi.finding: 145 recommendations. Diagnosis with disordered cycles for at least 4 months and a single FSH > 25 IU/l (repeat after 4–6 weeks only if there is uncertainty); AMH is not the primary diagnostic test. Karyotype and FMR1 premutation in all non-iatrogenic POI; 21-hydroxylase antibodies if the cause is unknown; TSH at diagnosis and every 5 years. Hormone therapy until the usual age of menopause, with or without symptoms; if the combined oral contraceptive is used, in a continuous or extended regimen. No intervention reliably increases natural conception; oocyte donation is the established option. Complementary therapies should not replace hormone therapy.
eshre-2024-poi.limitations: Recommendations and ⊕ symbols read in the Europe PMC open-access XML version of the summary article (PMC11631070); recommendation numbers, justifications and tables read in the full guideline (ESHRE PDF, 254 pp., where the ⊕ symbols do not extract). For most management options, POI-specific evidence is limited: almost 76% of the evidence-based recommendations are strong even where the evidence was limited to low or very low quality observational data; many recommendations are extrapolated from women at the usual age of menopause.

eta-2021-thyroid-art.title: 2021 European Thyroid Association Guideline on Thyroid Disorders prior to and during Assisted Reproduction
eta-2021-thyroid-art.authors: Poppe K, Bisschop P, Fugazzola L, Minziori G, Unuane D, Weghofer A
eta-2021-thyroid-art.population: Women and men in subfertile couples, before and during assisted reproduction (IVF/ICSI), in the European context. Aimed at endocrinologists and gynaecologists.
eta-2021-thyroid-art.finding: Screen TSH and TPOAb in every woman seeking advice for subfertility (R1; 1, ØØØO); TgAb if TSH > 2.5 mIU/L with negative TPOAb (R2). Defines subclinical hypothyroidism as TSH > 4.0 mIU/L or above the assay upper limit if that is higher; treat with levothyroxine to keep TSH < 2.5 mIU/L, with or without autoimmunity (R12, R13; 1, ØØOO). With autoimmunity and TSH between 2.5 and 4.0, low-dose levothyroxine (25–50 µg) case by case (R15; 2, ØØOO). Do not systematically treat euthyroid women with autoimmunity undergoing IVF/ICSI (R19; 2, ØØOO). Check TSH after stimulation in women with autoimmunity on levothyroxine (R17).
eta-2021-thyroid-art.limitations: Full text read on the PubMed Central HTML page (no pagination). Grades: 1 = strong recommendation, 2 = weak or suggestion; ØOOO very low to ØØØØ high quality. It predates ATA 2026 and the T4LIFE trial (2022), although it already includes TABLET and the Chinese IVF trial; its thresholds and its case-by-case levothyroxine stance in euthyroid autoimmunity differ from later guidelines.

nams-2022-hormone-therapy.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.authors: The 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Faubion SS (lead), Crandall CJ, Davis L, El Khoudary SR, Hodis HN, Lobo RA, Maki PM, Manson JE, Pinkerton JV, Santoro NF, Shifren JL, Shufelt CL, Thurston RC, Wolfman W
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.population: Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women considering hormone therapy, in the United States context (FDA indications). Position statement by an expert panel of The North American Menopause Society, approved by its Board of Trustees; Menopause 2022;29(7):767-794. Updates the 2017 statement.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.finding: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and prevents bone loss and fracture. In women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable; when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause it appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. Women with a uterus need adequate progestogen. It does not need to be routinely stopped at 60–65. Compounded “bioidentical” hormones raise safety concerns, and saliva or urine testing to set the dose is unreliable.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (28 pp.) read on the society's website. It is a consensus position statement, not a guideline with a formal systematic review: the “Key points” carry levels I (good and consistent evidence), II (limited or inconsistent) and III (consensus and expert opinion), with no separate strength grade. Much of the risk data comes from the WHI trials (oral conjugated equine estrogens and medroxyprogesterone acetate). US regulatory context. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026 (the society has published no later one).

nice-2021-ng197.title: Shared decision making. NICE guideline NG197
nice-2021-ng197.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2021-ng197.population: People using healthcare services and the professionals and organisations of the English health service (NHS); all decisions about tests, treatments and interventions.
nice-2021-ng197.finding: Shared decision making is a collaborative process in which a person and their healthcare professional work together to reach a joint decision. In practice: agree an agenda, explain the aims of each option, discuss openly the risks, benefits and consequences of each (including no treatment or no change), clarify what the person hopes to gain, give information in chunks and check understanding (teach back), give time, accept that their views may differ from the professional's, make a joint decision and agree when to review it, and make clear they can change their mind (1.2.7–1.2.16). To communicate risk: absolute rather than relative risk, natural frequencies, the same denominator, a defined time period and both positive and negative framing (1.4.5–1.4.11).
nice-2021-ng197.limitations: Full PDF read (32 pp., published 17 June 2021). It is an English health-service guideline: several recommendations are organisational (section 1.1) and are not cited here. The accompanying evidence reviews were not read.

nice-2024-ng73.title: Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (NG73)
nice-2024-ng73.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2024-ng73.population: Women and people with suspected or confirmed endometriosis, including those aged 17 and under, in the English health system. Published 6 Sep 2017; last updated 11 Nov 2024. Each recommendation carries the year it was written or changed ([2017], [2024], [2017, amended 2024]); NICE does not attach GRADE grades in the recommendation text.
nice-2024-ng73.finding: Offer transvaginal ultrasound to anyone with suspected endometriosis even if examination is normal (1.5.2); do not exclude endometriosis if examination and ultrasound are normal (1.5.4); do not use CA125 to diagnose it (1.5.8); consider specialist ultrasound or MRI for deep disease (1.5.9) and laparoscopy even if imaging is normal (1.5.11); refer to a specialist centre for endometrioma or deep disease (1.5.6); treat according to symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than stage (1.6.1). When fertility is a priority: offer excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis for disease not involving bowel, bladder or ureter (1.10.1); offer laparoscopic cystectomy or drainage and ablation of endometriomas, taking into account that drainage and ablation may preserve ovarian reserve more (1.10.2); discuss benefits and risks of surgery for deep endometriosis (1.10.3); do not offer hormonal treatment alone or with surgery to people trying to conceive (1.10.4). Does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1).
nice-2024-ng73.limitations: Read sections 1.5–1.10, the rationale for 1.10.2–1.10.4 and the context (full PDF, 33 pp.). The fertility recommendations are to be read alongside NICE NG257; the evidence on hormonal treatment combined with surgery is described as mixed. Evidence reviews A and B were not read. Guideline designed for the English health system.

nice-2026-ng23.title: Menopause: identification and management (NG23)
nice-2026-ng23.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng23.population: People in perimenopause and menopause in the UK health system; section 1.7 covers premature ovarian insufficiency in people under 40. Published November 2015, last updated 15 April 2026.
nice-2026-ng23.finding: From age 45, identify perimenopause (recently started vasomotor symptoms and cycle changes) and menopause (no period for 12 months without hormonal contraception) clinically, without laboratory tests; do not use AMH, inhibins, oestradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume [2015]. Offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms [2015]; consider menopause-specific CBT [2024]; fezolinetant when HRT is unsuitable (TA1143); do not routinely offer SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine as first-line treatment for vasomotor symptoms alone [2015]. Combined HRT with a uterus and oestrogen-only HRT after total hysterectomy, at the lowest effective dosage [2024], reviewed at 3 months and then annually [2015]. VTE risk is not increased with transdermal HRT but is with oral HRT; consider transdermal HRT if VTE risk is increased, including a BMI over 30 kg/m² [2015]. Breast cancer risk rises with combined HRT according to duration, and very little or not at all with oestrogen-only HRT [2024]. POI (1.7, 2015 recommendations): diagnosis with symptoms, including infrequent or absent periods, and raised FSH on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart; do not diagnose on a single blood test or use AMH routinely. Offer replacement with HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, until at least the age of natural menopause unless contraindicated; HRT may have a more beneficial effect on blood pressure than a combined oral contraceptive; both offer bone protection; HRT is not a contraceptive.
nice-2026-ng23.limitations: Full PDF (105 pp., 15-04-2026 version) read. The POI recommendations have not been updated since 2015 and predate the 2024 ESHRE guideline (which requires a single FSH). It gives no numerical FSH threshold. UK health-system context.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.title: Diagnosis and management of prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas: a Pituitary Society international Consensus Statement
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.authors: Petersenn S, Fleseriu M, Casanueva FF, Giustina A, Biermasz N, Biller BMK, Bronstein M, Chanson P, Fukuoka H, Gadelha M, Greenman Y, Gurnell M, Ho KKY, Honegger J, Ioachimescu AG, Kaiser UB, Karavitaki N, Katznelson L, Lodish M, Maiter D, Marcus HJ, McCormack A, Molitch M, Muir CA, Neggers S, Pereira AM, Pivonello R, Post K, Raverot G, Salvatori R, Samson SL, Shimon I, Spencer-Segal J, Vila G, Wass J, Melmed S
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.population: People with hyperprolactinaemia or prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (adults, pregnancy and fertility, children and adolescents, psychiatric disorders, menopause). International multidisciplinary Pituitary Society workshop with experts from 13 countries.
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.finding: Investigate prolactin with infertility, new menstrual irregularity, amenorrhoea or galactorrhoea (strong). With prolactin < 5 times the upper limit, repeat the measurement; use cannulated sampling if stress is suspected (strong). Review drugs, hypothyroidism, renal or liver failure and pregnancy (strong). Test macroprolactin when the rise is moderate (< 200 ng/ml), at least when clinical or imaging findings are discordant (strong); 1:100 dilution for a giant adenoma with normal or mildly raised prolactin (strong). MRI once hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed if no other cause is evident (strong). Cabergoline is the preferred agonist (strong). Echocardiography by dose (> 2.0 mg/week: baseline and every 2–3 years; ≤ 2.0 mg/week: after 5–6 years) (weak). Consider withdrawal with low doses, > 2 years of treatment and adenoma shrinkage (strong). Stop the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed (strong); do not use prolactin to monitor growth in pregnancy (strong); breastfeeding is usually not contraindicated (strong).
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.limitations: Full PDF read (Nat Rev Endocrinol 2023;19:722-740). Expert consensus by vote; grades “strong” (moderate or high evidence) and “weak” (low or very low) per Box 1 (p. 724), with no per-recommendation GRADE certainty. Literature up to January 2023. The supplementary boxes (including the pregnancy and withdrawal discussion) could not be read. Pituitary Society statement; not a fertility guideline.

porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.title: International consensus statement on microbiome testing in clinical practice
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.authors: Porcari S, Mullish BH, Asnicar F, Ng SC, Zhao L, Hansen R, O'Toole PW, Raes J, Hold G, Putignani L, et al.; Cammarota G, Gasbarrini A, Ianiro G
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.population: Microbiome testing (mainly gut) in clinical practice; 69 experts from 18 countries, Delphi consensus. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025;10(2):154-167.
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.finding: There is insufficient evidence to widely recommend routine microbiome testing (90%). It discourages direct patient requests without a clinical recommendation (80.4%), therapeutic advice from the provider (98%), the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio (86%), dysbiosis indices (90%) and strict healthy reference ranges (90%). Multiplex PCR and cultures are not microbiome testing (90%); vaginal samples should be processed according to existing evidence and indications (97.5%).
porcari-2025-microbiome-testing.limitations: The accepted author manuscript on PMC (PMC12343204) was read, not the typeset version; appendices not included. Expert-opinion statements (Delphi, ≥ 80% threshold), not GRADE recommendations; focused on the gut microbiome rather than vaginal or endometrial microbiome.

teede-2023-pcos-guideline.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.; International PCOS Network
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.finding: Graded recommendations (GRADE strength and certainty) on diagnosis (including AMH), glycaemic assessment, psychological management (screening, eating disorders, body image), lifestyle (diet, exercise, behavioural strategies, weight stigma), metformin, inositol and ovulation induction with letrozole.
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.limitations: Many recommendations with low or very low certainty; practice points and consensus recommendations carry no certainty rating.

uspstf-2023-folic-acid.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.population: People who plan to or could become pregnant (US); does not apply to those with a previous pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect or other very-high-risk situations.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.finding: Grade A: daily supplement containing 0.4–0.8 mg (400–800 µg) of folic acid, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first 2–3 months of pregnancy. No serious harms at usual doses; MTHFR variants are listed as a research need.
uspstf-2023-folic-acid.limitations: Statement read on the USPSTF website (full recommendation text); the JAMA evidence review was not read. US context with flour fortification; gives no dose for high risk.

who-2021-semen-manual.title: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, sixth edition
who-2021-semen-manual.population: Laboratory manual. Reference population (Campbell et al.): about 3500 men from 12 countries whose partners achieved a natural conception with time to pregnancy ≤12 months and 2–7 days of abstinence; excludes men attending infertility clinics. ISBN 978-92-4-003078-7.
who-2021-semen-manual.finding: Table 8.3 (5th centile; 95% CI): volume 1.4 ml (1.3–1.5); concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml (15–18); total number 39 × 10⁶/ejaculate (35–40); total motility 42% (40–43); progressive 30% (29–31); vitality 54% (50–56); normal forms 4% (3.9–4.0). The lower fifth centile does not represent a limit between fertile and infertile men (8.1.3); there is substantial overlap between them; the manual is not a guideline for clinical decisions and clinically useful decision limits are still lacking (8.1, 8.1.2.2). The 2–7-day abstinence recommendation is based on clinical experience and may contribute to variability (ch. 2). Distinguishing 3% from 5% normal forms in an individual requires assessing 1500 spermatozoa (ch. 2).
who-2021-semen-manual.limitations: Read in the text of the official WHO PDF (292 pages, copy in the source library): introduction 1.3; chapter 2 (factors influencing the ejaculate, 2–7-day abstinence, collection, counting and morphology); 3.2.1 (DNA fragmentation, as a technique and background only); and all of 8.1 with Tables 8.1–8.3 (pp. 211–213). Technical laboratory manual, not a clinical guideline; reference population of men whose partners conceived within ≤12 months, not of infertile couples; the manual calls these figures the “lower fifth percentile” (ESHRE and AUA/ASRM call them the fifth-percentile reference limit or lower reference limit). The remaining laboratory procedures were not read.
